title: Arguments, closures, and return behavior
outcome: Explain keyword forwarding and the difference between a proc and a lambda.
book: Language ch. 6; Eloquent Ruby ch. 18–20; Metaprogramming Ruby Wednesday

exercises.title: Find and fix the bug
exercises.prompt: A wrapper def call(*args); target(*args); end stops forwarding keywords correctly on a newer Ruby. Repair its signature and write a compatibility test.

exercises.title: Change one condition
exercises.prompt: A callback must return a value to a caller and continue the caller normally. Would you choose lambda or a proc with a non-local return?

trace.title: Positional args
trace.detail:
# The idea

A closure carries access to variables from its surrounding scope. It does not take a frozen snapshot of every value.

If that variable changes, the closure can see the new value. This is useful for callbacks and risky for long-lived captured state.

A lambda behaves like a small method: it checks argument count more strictly and return leaves the lambda.

A non-lambda proc can return from the method where it was defined; after that method has ended, such a return can raise LocalJumpError. Use lambdas when you want method-like callback behavior.

Ruby 2.7 is a transition version for keyword arguments. Code that forwards a final hash as keywords may warn there and fail on Ruby 3.

Be explicit about positional arguments, keyword arguments, and a block.

trace.title: Follow the middle steps
trace.detail:
Split the call into three envelopes: positional values in args, named values in kwargs, behavior in block. Forward each explicitly.

In Ruby 2.7, warnings are useful migration signals; do not silence them without understanding the call shape.

For the closure, reader keeps access to the label binding. Reassignment changes what that binding points to.

For a snapshot of text, create a separate value deliberately, such as label.dup.freeze when a shallow frozen string is what you need.

trace.title: Check the result
trace.detail: A callback with return inside Proc.new may exit its defining method rather than only finishing the callback. Rescue does not make confusing control flow easier to maintain.
